QUESTION 1: CURRENT FUNCTIONS AND DISTRI:
PKD Papar carries out disease surveillance and outbreak control, communicable disease prevention, vector control, environmental health, food safety, maternal and child health, school health, immunisation, NCD prevention, health promotion and emergency response. These services are delivered through the PKD and its network of Klinik Kesihatan, Klinik Desa, KKIA and Klinik Komuniti, in collaboration with hospitals, schools, local authorities and other agencies.
Papar has a mixed urban, semi-urban and rural population, including coastal and inland communities. The main factors affecting PKD work are the wide geographical coverage, distance between communities, seasonal flooding, growing population and different levels of access to health services. The district faces both communicable diseases, such as TB, dengue, HFMD and food poisoning, and non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes and hypertension. High-risk settings BWN housing area, Depot Imigresen, PUSPEN, Rumah Warga Tua Kinarut, Rumah Kanak-kanak Kinarut, flood prone area and food premises. Limited staff, increasing workload and the need to manage routine services while responding to outbreaks further increase the complexity of PKD work.
QUESTION 2: STRENGTHS:
The main strength of PKD Papar is the strong teamwork and cooperation among staff. Effective leadership provides clear direction from management to operational teams, allowing instructions and information to be communicated quickly. Staff from different units are also willing to support one another when additional manpower is needed.
PKD Papar has competent and experienced personnel with good technical skills and knowledge of the local communities. Surveillance data, notifications and field information are regularly reviewed to identify risks and guide action. For example, during outbreaks of food poisoning, HFMD or other communicable diseases, teams can be mobilised quickly to conduct investigations, control activities, health education and follow-up.
Resources such as staff, vehicles, equipment and supplies are managed according to current priorities. This allows PKD Papar to respond quickly and efficiently to disease outbreaks, floods, fires and other emergencies while continuing routine services.
Another important strength is the good collaboration with district agencies, including Hospital Papar, the District Office, local authorities, the Education Department, police, Fire and Rescue Department, Welfare Department and community leaders. The cooperation and trust from local communities also support contact tracing, outbreak investigations, health campaigns and community programmes. These combined strengths enable PKD Papar to deliver its public health functions effectively despite limited resources and a high workload.
QUESTION 3: WEAKNESSES:
PKD Papar continues to deliver its public health functions through good leadership, strong teamwork and support from other agencies and the community. However, service delivery is affected by major resource limitations.
The main challenge is a shortage of staff, especially in management, medical officers, medical assistants, nurses, pharmacy, laboratory and other support services. Many staff must handle several programmes at the same time, affecting routine services, outreach activities and outbreak response. Financial allocations, vehicles, equipment and other assets are also limited.
Some clinics are small and overcrowded, with insufficient space to meet increasing patient needs. The lack of X-ray services at clinics means patients must be referred elsewhere, causing delays and additional travel. PKD Papar also lacks expertise in digital health and data management, while some work still depends on manual or separate systems.
Additional staff, funding, assets, better facilities, diagnostic services and digital expertise are needed for PKD Papar to fulfil its public health mandate more effectively.
QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
The implementation of CCMS in clinics is an important opportunity for PKD Papar. It can improve patient records, data quality, continuity of care and service efficiency.
The rapid development of Papar also creates opportunities to expand and upgrade health facilities, digital infrastructure and public health services to meet the needs of a growing population.
Health system reforms may provide clearer responsibilities and better allocation of staff, funding and assets. Staff training in digital health, data analysis, leadership and outbreak management can strengthen workforce competency.
Closer collaboration with Hospital Papar, UMS, district agencies, schools, NGOs, the private sector and community leaders can also support health programmes, research and emergency response.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
Future challenges for PKD Papar include rapid population growth, urbanisation and the increasing non-citizen population, which may raise demand for health services. Population mobility, communication barriers and difficulties with documentation may also affect immunisation, disease surveillance, contact tracing and treatment follow-up.
Changing disease patterns and outbreaks, such as dengue, HFMD, tuberculosis, food poisoning and emerging infections, may further increase workload. Climate change, floods and extreme weather may also increase the risk of disasters and infectious diseases.
Other threats include the increasing burden of non-communicable diseases, health misinformation, and rising community expectations. Limited staff, funding, assets and clinic capacity may reduce PKD Papar’s ability to manage these challenges effectively.

QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
One of the most powerful opportunities to strengthen the future role and performance of District Health Offices (PKD) lies in the adoption of advanced digital technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI can transform PKD operations by enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and responsiveness in several key areas:

Data-Driven Decision Making: AI-powered analytics can integrate surveillance, patient records, and service utilization data into real-time dashboards. This allows PKD to detect disease trends earlier, allocate resources more effectively, and design targeted interventions.

Operational Efficiency: AI can automate routine administrative tasks such as scheduling, reporting, and workload analysis. This reduces staff burden and frees up human resources for direct service delivery.

Predictive Health Intelligence: Machine learning models can forecast outbreaks, anticipate service demand, and identify high-risk populations. PKD can then act proactively rather than reactively.

Community Engagement: AI-enabled chatbots and digital platforms can provide health education, appointment reminders, and feedback channels, strengthening PKD’s relationship with the community.

Workforce Development: AI-driven training tools and simulations can upskill staff in epidemiology, digital literacy, and health financing, ensuring a more competent and future-ready workforce.

Service Innovation: Telehealth platforms enhanced by AI can extend PKD’s reach to underserved populations, while AI-assisted diagnostics can improve the quality of care at the primary level.

By strategically embedding AI into its operations, PKD can evolve from being primarily a program implementer into a smart health system leader at the district level—capable of delivering more responsive, equitable, and sustainable public health services.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
An important external challenge that may affect the ability of District Health Offices (PKD) to protect and improve population health is the lack of clarity and contextual relevance in policies and directives issued by the Ministry of Health headquarters (KKM HQ).

When policies are communicated in a vague manner or designed without considering the unique realities at the district level, they often become difficult to interpret, misaligned with local needs, and impractical to implement. This results in operational confusion, delays in execution, and reduced effectiveness of health programs.

For example, a directive intended for urban districts may not be suitable for rural or resource-constrained areas, yet PKD is still expected to comply. Such mismatches weaken the ability of PKD to respond flexibly to local health challenges and undermine community trust in public health services.

To address this, future reforms should emphasize clearer guidance, participatory policy design, and adaptive frameworks that allow PKD to tailor implementation strategies to their specific district context while still aligning with national priorities.

QUESTION 1: CURRENT FUNCTIONS AND DISTRI: PKD Kuala Nerus provides all the basic Public Health functions, from Disease Prevention and Control (Unit Inspektorat) to Primary Care in which programs covers the Womb to Tomb entities, through 4 health clinics and 10 rural clinics and Pre-Hospital Care Services. Thus the scope of disease surveillance and emergency preparedness surrounds high-transit population and areas.
QUESTION 2: STRENGTHS: PKDKN is now 10 years into it's establishment. PKDKN is well known among community leaders and an important agency within the District Office and State Government. Most implementation of Public Health programs are able to transcend via collaboration between governmental and non-governmental agencies, including the 2 main universities.

PKDKN headquarters operates from a converted ILKKM facilities, key administrative and public health units operated in dispersed and makeshift spaces. Climate Change, Rising Sea Levels, and Severe Monsoon Disasters - yearly flooding episodes, constant coastal erosions increases public health threats and further damages vulnerable facilities. 2. Rapid Urbanization, Commercial developments and Demographic Shifts - Unplanned urban density creates risk for vector borne diseases, A shifting demographic profile—combining a large young student population with an aging local population—demands simultaneous management of lifestyle-related Non-Communicable Diseases (Diabetes, Hypertension) alongside youth and adolescent health needs (Social behaviour related communicable diseases - HIV, STDs). 3. QUESTION 2: STRENGTHS:
The main strengths of our PKD that enable it to deliver its public health functions effectively include:
Skilled and committed workforce – Our multidisciplinary team, comprising medical officers, public health specialists, nurses, environmental health officers, and support staff, works collaboratively to provide comprehensive public health services. For example, the team successfully coordinates outbreak investigations, immunization programmes, and maternal and child health services.
Strong disease surveillance and response system – The PKD has established surveillance mechanisms for the early detection and reporting of communicable diseases. For example, rapid response teams conduct timely investigations and implement control measures during dengue, food poisoning, or COVID-19 outbreaks.
Effective collaboration with stakeholders – The PKD works closely with hospitals, schools, local authorities, community leaders, and non-governmental organizations to implement health promotion and disease prevention activities. For example, joint dengue control campaigns and school health programmes have improved community participation.
Comprehensive primary healthcare network – Supported by health clinics and community clinics, the PKD ensures accessible preventive and promotive health services, including immunization, antenatal care, non-communicable disease screening, and health education.
Strong community engagement – Community volunteers and local leaders actively participate in public health initiatives, such as health awareness campaigns, vector control activities, and emergency response, helping to improve programme coverage and public trust.
QUESTION 3: WEAKNESSES: PKD also faces several challenges that limit its effectiveness. Workforce shortages and increasing workloads often reduce the capacity to carry out preventive and outreach activities. Budget constraints may delay health promotion programmes or environmental health interventions. Rising numbers of non-communicable diseases, an ageing population, and recurring outbreaks of communicable diseases further increase service demands. In some communities, vaccine hesitancy and low participation in health screening programmes reduce the impact of preventive health initiatives. Additionally, geographical barriers in remote areas may affect timely access to healthcare services and public health interventions.
QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
The increasing use of digital health technologies provides significant opportunities to strengthen disease surveillance, data analysis, and service delivery. Digital reporting systems, electronic medical records, mobile health applications, and data dashboards can support real-time monitoring of disease trends, improve decision-making, and enable more targeted public health interventions.
Greater inter-agency collaboration offers another important opportunity. Strengthening partnerships with local authorities, hospitals, educational institutions, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), and community leaders can improve responses to public health issues such as dengue prevention, food safety, outbreak investigations, and health promotion. Multi-sectoral collaboration also helps address the social determinants of health more effectively.
The growing emphasis on community engagement and health literacy provides an opportunity to empower communities to take a more active role in disease prevention and healthy lifestyle practices. Expanding the use of social media, digital campaigns, and community volunteers can increase public awareness, improve vaccination uptake, encourage health screening participation, and strengthen outbreak preparedness.
The adoption of data-driven public health planning can further improve resource allocation and programme effectiveness. By analysing local epidemiological data and health indicators, the PKD can identify priority populations, monitor programme performance, and implement evidence-based interventions tailored to community needs.
Finally, continued capacity building and workforce development present an opportunity to strengthen the competencies of public health personnel. Regular training in epidemiology, emergency preparedness, digital health, leadership, and quality improvement will enable staff to respond more effectively to emerging health challenges, including climate-related health risks and future pandemics.
By leveraging these opportunities, the PKD can become more proactive, resilient, and responsive, ensuring that essential public health services remain effective and sustainable while meeting the evolving health needs of the population.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
Several external threats and emerging challenges may affect the PKD's ability to protect and improve population health in the coming years.
One of the most significant threats is climate change, which is expected to increase the frequency of floods, heatwaves, and extreme weather events. These conditions may contribute to higher incidences of vector-borne diseases such as dengue and malaria, waterborne diseases following floods, and heat-related illnesses. For example, prolonged heavy rainfall can create more mosquito breeding sites, leading to dengue outbreaks that require intensive vector control and surveillance activities.
The increasing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and cardiovascular diseases, presents another major challenge. An ageing population and unhealthy lifestyles will increase demand for chronic disease prevention, screening, and long-term management, placing additional pressure on PKD resources and workforce capacity.
The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases remain an ongoing threat. Future outbreaks or pandemics similar to COVID-19, as well as diseases such as measles, influenza, mpox, or antimicrobial-resistant infections, may require rapid mobilisation of public health resources for surveillance, contact tracing, vaccination, and risk communication while maintaining routine health services.
Another challenge is vaccine hesitancy and health misinformation, particularly through social media platforms. The spread of false information can reduce vaccination coverage, increase community resistance to public health interventions, and make outbreak control more difficult. For example, declining childhood immunisation rates may increase the risk of measles outbreaks.
Population growth, urbanisation, and migration may also place additional demands on healthcare services. Rapid urban development can contribute to overcrowding, environmental health issues, and increased transmission of communicable diseases, while migrant and hard-to-reach populations may face barriers in accessing preventive health services.
Finally, resource constraints, including limited funding, shortages of trained public health personnel, and increasing operational costs, may reduce the PKD's capacity to implement preventive programmes, conduct inspections, and respond effectively to emergencies.
To address these threats, the PKD should strengthen emergency preparedness, invest in digital surveillance systems, enhance workforce capacity, promote community engagement, and foster stronger collaboration with other government agencies, local authorities, academic institutions, and community organisations. These strategies will improve resilience and ensure that the PKD remains capable of protecting population health despite future challenges.
Additional Comments (Optional):
An important issue that should be considered in the PKD transformation initiative is ensuring that the transformation is supported by adequate resources, clear governance, and effective change management. While new policies and digital innovations are important, their success depends on sufficient staffing, continuous training, reliable infrastructure, and manageable workloads. Transformation should enhance service delivery without creating additional administrative burdens for frontline healthcare workers.
Another key consideration is strengthening collaboration between the PKD, hospitals, primary care clinics, local authorities, educational institutions, and community organisations. A more integrated and coordinated health system will enable faster responses to public health emergencies, better management of chronic diseases, and more effective health promotion activities.
My expectation is that the PKD transformation initiative will create a more modern, data-driven, and people-centred public health system. The PKD should be empowered with stronger digital capabilities, improved workforce capacity, sustainable funding, and greater autonomy to respond to local public health needs. Continuous professional development and staff well-being should also be prioritised to maintain a motivated and resilient workforce.
Ultimately, I hope the transformation will strengthen the PKD's role as the frontline public health authority, capable of preventing disease, responding rapidly to emerging health threats, reducing health inequalities, and improving the overall health and well-being of the communities it serves. By investing in prevention, innovation, and community partnerships, the PKD will be better positioned to meet future public health challenges and achieve better health outcomes for all.

Pejabat Kesihatan Kawasan Kinabatangan delivers public health and primary healthcare services across Kinabatangan and Tongod. Functions include disease surveillance and outbreak control, vector control, tuberculosis and leprosy services, immunisation, maternal and child health, school health, NCD prevention, nutrition, environmental health, food safety, occupational health, health promotion and disaster response.

The main challenge is geography. Both districts cover more than 16,000 square kilometres, with communities dispersed across villages, plantations, riverine settlements and remote interior areas. Some locations require several hours or a full day of travel by road, four-wheel-drive vehicle or boat.

The population is diverse and mobile, including plantation workers, non-citizens and remote communities. Frequent movement, incomplete records and uncertain immunisation status can complicate contact tracing, tuberculosis treatment, maternal care and chronic disease follow-up.

The district also faces a double burden of communicable diseases such as dengue, malaria, tuberculosis, measles, diphtheria, typhoid and food poisoning, together with rising diabetes, hypertension, obesity and mental health problems.

Facilities are widely separated and vary in staffing, infrastructure and connectivity. Overall workload is influenced not only by population size, but also by remoteness, travel time, accessibility, disease burden and the cost of reaching underserved communities.
QUESTION 2: STRENGTHS:
The main strengths of the PKK are responsive leadership, committed staff, multidisciplinary teamwork, strong local knowledge and effective collaboration.

The PKK can rapidly coordinate clinics, surveillance, environmental health, laboratories, hospitals and external agencies during outbreaks, disasters and environmental incidents.

Staff are adaptable and often manage routine services, field investigations, outreach and reporting within the same day. Strong teamwork supports comprehensive responses, such as combining epidemiological investigation, vector control, health education and community mobilisation during dengue outbreaks.

Local knowledge of villages, plantations, rivers, roads and community leaders helps teams plan outreach and trace contacts effectively.

The PKK also uses surveillance trends, locality mapping and screening data to guide action. Strong relationships with communities, schools, plantation management and agencies support immunisation, outbreak control, health promotion and disaster response.
QUESTION 3: WEAKNESSES:
The main weaknesses are structural and operational.

Resource allocation does not fully reflect the large geographical area, difficult access and higher cost of service delivery. A single field visit may require an entire day, repeated travel or overnight deployment.

Workforce capacity is stretched because many officers manage multiple programmes. During outbreaks or disasters, staff are redeployed from routine activities, affecting supervision, screening and programme evaluation.

Some functions depend heavily on a small number of experienced officers. Data systems are fragmented across different platforms and manual reports, causing duplicated work and limiting deeper analysis.

Specimen transport, laboratory feedback and referrals may be delayed by distance. Public health operations are also vulnerable to vehicle or boat breakdowns, poor roads, floods and slow procurement processes.

Remote facilities have uneven infrastructure and internet connectivity. The PKK also has limited authority over wider issues such as drainage, waste management, housing, water supply and plantation conditions.
QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
The PKD transformation initiative offers an opportunity to strengthen district-level authority and capacity.

Resource allocation should consider geography, travel time, accessibility, disease risk and population mobility, not population size alone.

Greater district authority, emergency funds and simplified approval processes would allow faster responses during outbreaks and disasters.

Integrated digital systems and district dashboards could combine surveillance, laboratory, clinic and programme data. Offline-capable platforms would support remote clinics.

GIS mapping could identify disease hotspots, flood-prone areas, remote settlements and transport routes to improve outreach and preparedness.

Workforce development should strengthen epidemiology, data analysis, risk communication and emergency management. Community networks, plantation partnerships and multisectoral collaboration could support early warning, health promotion and follow-up.

Service innovations such as integrated outreach, boat clinics, mobile teams and telehealth could improve access for remote communities.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
Future threats are likely to become more complex and occur simultaneously.

Communicable diseases will remain important while NCDs, obesity, mental health conditions and population ageing increase.

Outbreak control may become harder because of migration, incomplete immunisation, remote settlements, delayed healthcare-seeking and slow specimen transport.

Population movement involving plantation workers, non-citizens and mobile families may disrupt immunisation, tuberculosis treatment, maternal care and contact tracing.

Urbanisation, plantation expansion and land-use change may increase overcrowding, sanitation problems, dengue risk and human–wildlife contact.

Climate change may increase floods, heat, drought, fires, landslides and water disruption. These can isolate communities, delay referrals, interrupt medicines and increase infectious disease risk.

Misinformation may contribute to vaccine hesitancy, delayed treatment and reduced trust. Community expectations may also exceed available staffing, transport, facilities and connectivity.

The greatest threat is the possibility of outbreaks, disasters and routine service demands occurring at the same time.

For large rural districts, staffing, funding and performance indicators should reflect geography, accessibility, population mobility and service complexity.

My hope is for a more empowered, data-driven and flexible PKD with stronger district authority, integrated systems, resilient logistics and adequate multidisciplinary staffing.

QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
1. Digital Health Transformation and Data Integration

The expansion of digital health systems offers significant opportunities to improve disease surveillance, service planning, and operational efficiency. Integrating electronic medical records, public health surveillance platforms, laboratory reporting, and real-time dashboards will enable earlier detection of outbreaks, better monitoring of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and more targeted public health interventions. Artificial intelligence and predictive analytics can further support risk stratification, resource allocation, and proactive public health decision-making.

2. Strengthening Public–Private Collaboration

Kuantan has a well-developed private healthcare sector comprising private hospitals, general practitioner (GP) clinics, community pharmacies, occupational health providers, and industries. Strengthening partnerships with these providers can substantially expand access to preventive services and improve continuity of care.

Private practitioners can play a greater role in:

* Immunisation programmes for children and adults.
* NCD screening, risk assessment, and long-term management.
* Mental health screening and referral.
* Early notification of communicable diseases and outbreak surveillance.
* Health promotion and lifestyle counselling.
* Shared care for stable chronic disease patients.

Establishing stronger data-sharing mechanisms, referral pathways, and joint quality improvement initiatives between public and private sectors would create a more integrated district health system.

3. National Health Insurance and Health Financing Reform

The proposed National Health Insurance or broader health financing reforms present an important opportunity to redesign healthcare delivery. If implemented, PKD Kuantan could transition from being primarily a direct provider of services to becoming a district population health manager and system coordinator.

Through strategic purchasing and empanelment of both public and private providers, primary healthcare services could become more accessible while reducing congestion in government facilities. Financing reforms could support integrated chronic disease management, preventive health services, and value-based care, where providers are incentivised based on quality and health outcomes rather than service volume. This would strengthen equity, efficiency, and continuity of care across the district.

4. Workforce Development and Leadership

The increasing complexity of public health challenges requires continuous investment in workforce development. Strengthening competencies in epidemiology, digital health, health economics, implementation science, emergency preparedness, behavioural science, and health leadership will improve organisational resilience.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams involving family medicine specialists, pharmacists, environmental health officers, nutritionists, psychologists, and allied health professionals will enhance integrated service delivery. Leadership development programmes for future public health leaders will ensure sustainable succession planning.

5. Community Empowerment and Community Networks

Existing community platforms such as Agenda Nasional Malaysia Sihat (ANMS), Komuniti Bebas Denggi (KomBeD), Village Health Volunteers, Resident Associations, schools, and religious organisations provide strong foundations for community participation.

Greater community ownership of health initiatives can improve prevention of dengue, obesity, diabetes, mental health issues, and tobacco use while strengthening disaster preparedness. Digital communication platforms and social media can further enhance health literacy and public engagement.

6. Multisectoral Partnerships

As the economic hub of Pahang, Kuantan hosts major industries including the Gebeng Industrial Estate, Malaysia–China Kuantan Industrial Park (MCKIP), Kuantan Port, and the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) project.

Closer collaboration with local authorities, industries, educational institutions, environmental agencies, and non-governmental organisations can strengthen occupational health, environmental monitoring, emergency preparedness, climate resilience, and workplace health promotion. A Health in All Policies (HiAP) approach would enable health considerations to be integrated into urban planning, transport, housing, and industrial development.

7. Research, Innovation, and Implementation Science

PKD Kuantan is well positioned to become a district-level centre for operational research and implementation science through collaborations with universities and research institutions.

Routine use of programme evaluation, geospatial analysis, behavioural research, and implementation studies would generate local evidence to improve service delivery and inform policy. Innovative models of care, including telehealth, digital monitoring, and community-based interventions, should be evaluated and scaled where effective.

8. Service Innovation and Integrated Primary Healthcare

Future healthcare delivery should move towards integrated, person-centred, and preventive models of care. Digital consultations, remote patient monitoring, home-based care for frail older adults, multidisciplinary NCD clinics, and stronger integration between preventive and curative services can improve accessibility while reducing unnecessary hospital utilisation.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
1. Rapid Urbanisation and Population Growth

As the state capital and economic hub of Pahang, Kuantan continues to experience rapid urbanisation and population growth. Large-scale developments, including the Malaysia–China Kuantan Industrial Park (MCKIP), Kuantan Port expansion, and the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL), have increased population mobility and migration. These changes place greater demand on primary healthcare services, environmental health monitoring, communicable disease surveillance, and health promotion activities.

2. Changing Disease Patterns

PKD Kuantan is managing a dual burden of disease. While communicable diseases such as dengue, tuberculosis, hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD), measles, and food- and water-borne diseases continue to require intensive surveillance and rapid response, the prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, chronic kidney disease, and cancer continues to rise. This increases demand for long-term preventive care, screening, and integrated chronic disease management.

3. Climate Change and Extreme Weather Events

Climate change presents an increasing public health threat. Kuantan is particularly vulnerable to the northeast monsoon, which frequently causes flooding. Floods disrupt healthcare services, damage infrastructure, affect water and sanitation systems, increase the risk of communicable disease outbreaks, and require extensive public health emergency response. Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns may also increase mosquito breeding and prolong dengue transmission.

4. Emerging and Re-emerging Infectious Diseases

The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated the importance of maintaining strong public health preparedness. Future emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance, zoonotic infections, and imported diseases due to increased international travel remain significant threats. Maintaining laboratory capacity, surveillance systems, and rapid response teams will continue to be essential.

5. Population Ageing

An ageing population will increase demand for chronic disease management, rehabilitation, palliative care, home-based services, mental health support, and caregiver assistance. Primary healthcare services must evolve to provide more integrated and person-centred care for older adults with multiple chronic conditions.

6. Misinformation and Declining Public Trust

The rapid spread of misinformation through social media presents an increasing challenge. False information regarding vaccination, communicable diseases, nutrition, and public health interventions may reduce community compliance and undermine disease prevention efforts. PKD Kuantan will need to strengthen risk communication, community engagement, and digital health education to maintain public confidence.

7. Workforce and Resource Constraints

Increasing service demand without proportional growth in workforce, infrastructure, and financial resources may affect service quality and responsiveness. Recruitment and retention of skilled healthcare workers, ageing healthcare facilities, and competing healthcare priorities may place additional pressure on district health services.

8. Industrialisation and Environmental Health Risks

Kuantan’s expanding industrial sector, including the Gebeng Industrial Estate, Kuantan Port, and MCKIP, increases the need for environmental health surveillance and emergency preparedness. Potential industrial accidents, hazardous chemical exposure, air and water pollution, and occupational health risks require strong collaboration between the Ministry of Health, local authorities, industries, and environmental agencies.

9. Increasing Community Expectations

Communities increasingly expect healthcare services that are timely, accessible, digitally enabled, and patient-centred. Meeting these expectations while maintaining equitable access, particularly for rural and Orang Asli communities, will require continuous service innovation, digital transformation, and stronger collaboration with private healthcare providers.

Close cooperation between clinical and public health teams facilitates integrated service delivery, efficient programme implementation, rapid outbreak response, and coordinated emergency management. This collaborative working culture strengthens organisational resilience and enables multidisciplinary approaches to increasingly complex health issues.

Beyond the health sector, PKD Kemaman has established excellent interagency collaboration with local authorities, emergency services, educational institutions, industry partners, community leaders, non-governmental organisations, and other government agencies. These longstanding partnerships greatly facilitate health promotion activities, outbreak investigations, environmental health interventions, disaster preparedness, emergency response, and implementation of public health programmes. During seasonal flooding and other emergencies, these collaborative relationships enable rapid mobilisation of resources, coordinated decision-making, and effective multisectoral response to protect community health.

Overall, the combination of a strategically distributed healthcare network, an experienced and competent workforce, supportive leadership, a strong culture of mentorship, operational flexibility, effective teamwork, and robust interagency collaboration forms the foundation of PKD Kemaman's ability to deliver comprehensive, responsive, and high-quality public health services despite increasing service demands and workforce constraints.
QUESTION 3: WEAKNESSES:
PKD Kemaman continues to fulfil its public health mandate despite operating in an increasingly demanding environment characterised by growing healthcare needs, expanding public expectations, and resource limitations. While the district benefits from experienced personnel, effective leadership, and strong interagency collaboration, several structural and operational constraints continue to affect the efficiency, sustainability, and quality of service delivery.

One of the most significant challenges is the limited physical capacity of healthcare facilities. Many offices, health clinics, community clinics, stores, meeting rooms, and clinical workspaces were designed for considerably smaller populations and lower service volumes than those currently served. As the district population and healthcare demand have increased, many facilities have become overcrowded, affecting patient flow, staff productivity, confidentiality during consultations, storage of medical supplies, and the flexibility required to introduce new public health programmes or services. In several facilities, administrative staff and healthcare personnel work within constrained office environments that limit efficient workflow and multidisciplinary collaboration.

The condition of ageing infrastructure and equipment presents another major operational challenge. Several healthcare facilities require upgrading or refurbishment to meet current operational requirements. In addition, ageing medical equipment, information technology hardware, ambulances, operational vehicles, and other essential assets are increasingly difficult to maintain. Many computers are outdated and operate below current software requirements, affecting data processing, reporting, virtual meetings, and access to digital health systems. Operational vehicles and ambulances require frequent maintenance, while some medical equipment has exceeded its recommended service life and should be replaced under government asset replacement programmes. However, delays in procurement and replacement approvals often prolong the use of ageing assets beyond their intended lifespan, reducing operational reliability, increasing maintenance costs, and occasionally disrupting service delivery.

Human resource sustainability has become another major concern. Although the district has an approved workforce establishment that is generally sufficient to support both district-level public health functions and service delivery across healthcare facilities, many established positions remain vacant. Over recent years, a considerable number of experienced staff have retired without timely replacement due to limited recruitment. At the same time, the resignation of medical officers to pursue opportunities in the private sector, together with the transition of contract officers to permanent appointments in other locations, has further reduced the available workforce within the district. These workforce movements have created additional pressure on remaining personnel, requiring many officers to assume multiple responsibilities beyond their primary roles.

Beyond workforce numbers, these staffing changes have also resulted in the gradual loss of valuable institutional memory, technical expertise, and leadership experience. Senior personnel who have accumulated extensive knowledge of district operations, local epidemiology, emergency response, and programme implementation are not always replaced by staff with equivalent experience. Consequently, existing senior officers spend considerable time mentoring and supervising newly appointed personnel while simultaneously maintaining routine service delivery, placing additional demands on already limited human resources.

Increasing service demand has further intensified workload across both public health and primary healthcare services. PKD Kemaman not only serves its resident population but also supports a highly mobile industrial workforce associated with the oil and gas sector, manufacturing industries, and offshore operations. This creates additional responsibilities in communicable disease surveillance, occupational health, environmental health, disaster preparedness, emergency response, and public health programme implementation. New national initiatives, expanded reporting requirements, and increasing public expectations have further increased administrative and operational workloads without proportional expansion of infrastructure or workforce capacity.

The district is also undergoing an important transition towards greater digitalisation of healthcare services. However, ageing information technology infrastructure, inconsistent availability of modern hardware, and increasing dependence on multiple digital reporting systems can reduce efficiency rather than improve it. Staff frequently need to navigate numerous reporting platforms and duplicate documentation requirements, increasing administrative burden and reducing the time available for direct public health interventions and community engagement.

Geographical diversity further complicates service delivery. Healthcare teams are required to serve urban populations, coastal communities, industrial areas, FELDA settlements, plantations, mining sites, logging areas, and remote inland villages. During the annual northeast monsoon, flooding and road disruptions can affect accessibility, outreach activities, environmental health operations, disease surveillance, and continuity of healthcare services. These circumstances require extensive contingency planning and flexible deployment of personnel and resources.

Despite these operational constraints, PKD Kemaman continues to maintain effective public health services through the dedication and professionalism of its workforce, strong teamwork, experienced leadership, and close collaboration with the Terengganu State Health Department and local partner agencies. Nevertheless, sustaining high-quality public health services in the future will require continued investment in healthcare infrastructure, timely replacement of ageing assets, strengthening of digital capabilities, expansion of healthcare facilities, and a sustainable workforce strategy that addresses recruitment, retention, succession planning, and preservation of institutional expertise. These improvements are essential to ensure that the district remains capable of meeting the increasing healthcare needs of its growing resident population and highly mobile industrial workforce.
QUESTION 4: OPPORTUNITIES:
PKD Kemaman has several important opportunities to strengthen its future role by building upon its established leadership, experienced workforce, strong interagency relationships, strategically distributed healthcare facilities, and extensive experience in managing both routine public health programmes and complex emergencies. These opportunities are particularly relevant because Kemaman faces a unique combination of industrial, maritime, environmental, demographic, and behavioural health risks that require an integrated, adaptive, and forward-looking public health system.

One significant opportunity is to strengthen the role of PKD Kemaman as a district-level coordinator for emerging public health threats. A current example is the increasing detection of new psychoactive substances concealed in electronic cigarette (vape) products. This emerging issue presents new challenges for healthcare providers, law enforcement agencies, and regulatory authorities because clinical presentation, laboratory confirmation, legal classification, and enforcement procedures are still evolving. Consequently, coordinated responses are required across multiple sectors.

At district level, PKD Kemaman has utilised the Mesyuarat Tindakan Membanteras Dadah (MTMD) as a multisectoral platform to discuss emerging cases involving suspected substance-containing vape products. Through this mechanism, agencies such as PKD, the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM), the National Anti-Drug Agency (AADK), hospital services, laboratories, educational institutions, and local authorities are able to develop common approaches for case detection, laboratory testing, evidence management, referral pathways, risk communication, and enforcement actions. This collaborative approach enables new public health threats to be addressed systematically while ensuring that healthcare, public safety, and legal considerations remain aligned.

Another important opportunity is to further develop PKD Kemaman as a centre of excellence for public health emergency preparedness and disaster management. The district has accumulated extensive operational experience in responding to annual northeast monsoon floods, evacuation centre operations, continuity of healthcare services, communicable disease surveillance during disasters, environmental health interventions, and coordinated emergency response. In addition to seasonal flooding, the district has also managed sudden natural disasters, water-related incidents, and industrial emergencies requiring rapid mobilisation of multiple agencies.

The strategic location of Kemaman as one of Malaysia's major oil and gas hubs provides an additional opportunity to strengthen collaboration with industrial partners. The presence of offshore platforms, petrochemical industries, oil terminals, the Kemaman Supply Base, and Kemaman Port requires continuous preparedness for industrial accidents, hazardous material incidents, gas leaks, marine emergencies, and mass casualty events. These industrial risks necessitate close collaboration between healthcare services, emergency responders, industry operators, environmental agencies, and local authorities.

A major strength of the district is the long-standing culture of multisectoral collaboration. Regular emergency drills involving government agencies, PETRONAS, oil and gas companies, port operators, emergency services, and other private industries have significantly enhanced district preparedness. These exercises allow agencies to test command structures, communication pathways, resource mobilisation, evacuation procedures, casualty management, environmental health responses, and business continuity planning. More importantly, each exercise provides valuable lessons that can be translated into improvements in standard operating procedures, emergency response plans, and future preparedness activities.

PKD Kemaman also has an excellent opportunity to strengthen public health intelligence through digital transformation. The increasing availability of electronic health information, disease surveillance systems, geographic information systems (GIS), and digital reporting platforms provides opportunities to integrate information from communicable diseases, non-communicable diseases, environmental health, occupational health, Port Health, disaster management, and healthcare services into a comprehensive district public health dashboard. Such a system would support evidence-based decision-making, early detection of outbreaks, monitoring of vulnerable populations, resource allocation, and rapid emergency response.

Another important opportunity lies in workforce development and succession planning. Although PKD Kemaman currently benefits from many experienced officers with extensive technical expertise, a structured competency development programme would ensure that valuable institutional knowledge is transferred to younger staff before senior officers retire. Formal mentoring programmes, simulation exercises, competency-based training, cross-unit attachments, and multidisciplinary learning activities would strengthen future workforce capability while maintaining service quality and organisational resilience.

Community engagement also presents significant opportunities for future public health improvement. Kemaman has well-established relationships with community leaders, schools, industries, FELDA settlements, non-governmental organisations, and volunteer groups. These networks can be further strengthened to support health promotion, behavioural change programmes, early disease detection, disaster preparedness, substance abuse prevention, mental health initiatives, and community-based surveillance. Active community participation enables public health interventions to be more responsive, culturally appropriate, and sustainable.

Finally, the decentralised decision-making approach adopted by the Terengganu State Health Department provides PKD Kemaman with valuable flexibility to introduce district-specific innovations. This autonomy enables local leadership to respond rapidly to emerging public health challenges, pilot new service delivery models, strengthen multisectoral collaboration, and implement solutions tailored to the unique needs of the district.
QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
PKD Kemaman is expected to face increasingly complex external threats over the coming years as demographic changes, rapid industrial development, climate change, technological advancement, and evolving disease patterns continue to reshape public health priorities. As a district with strategic industrial importance and a highly mobile population, these emerging challenges will require more integrated, adaptive, and evidence-based public health approaches.

One of the most significant threats is the changing epidemiological profile of the population. While communicable diseases remain an important public health concern, the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) continues to increase due to population ageing, unhealthy lifestyles, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and chronic kidney disease. Managing this dual burden requires substantial healthcare resources while maintaining preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks and other public health emergencies.

Kemaman's role as one of Malaysia's major oil and gas and industrial hubs presents unique public health challenges. The continuous movement of interstate workers, offshore personnel, expatriates, foreign workers, and contractors increases the risk of imported infectious diseases, occupational health incidents, environmental exposures, and industrial emergencies. Future public health planning must therefore extend beyond the resident population and incorporate surveillance strategies that account for this highly mobile workforce.

Climate change represents another major emerging threat. Kemaman experiences recurrent northeast monsoon flooding, with increasing rainfall intensity and more unpredictable weather patterns affecting healthcare accessibility, environmental sanitation, vector breeding, water quality, mental well-being, and continuity of healthcare services. Future climate-related events may become more frequent and severe, requiring greater investment in disaster preparedness, early warning systems, resilient healthcare infrastructure, and coordinated multisectoral emergency response.

The district's concentration of petrochemical industries, offshore platforms, oil terminals, pipelines, and port facilities also exposes the population to potential technological and industrial hazards. Although major incidents are uncommon, events such as chemical releases, gas leaks, industrial fires, marine pollution, transportation accidents involving hazardous materials, or mass casualty incidents could have significant public health consequences. These risks require continuous preparedness, regular emergency exercises, and close collaboration between health authorities, emergency responders, industry operators, and environmental agencies.

Another emerging challenge is the rapid evolution of substance use behaviours, particularly the misuse of electronic cigarettes (vapes) containing illicit or synthetic psychoactive substances. These products pose new clinical, laboratory, legal, and enforcement challenges because they may not be easily detected using conventional approaches. Addressing this issue will require stronger surveillance systems, laboratory capability, health education, policy adaptation, and close collaboration with enforcement agencies and educational institutions.

The increasing spread of health misinformation and disinformation through social media also threatens effective public health practice. False information regarding vaccination, infectious diseases, chronic disease management, medications, and emerging health threats may reduce public confidence in evidence-based interventions, delay healthcare seeking behaviour, and contribute to vaccine hesitancy or poor treatment adherence. Public health agencies must therefore strengthen risk communication, digital engagement, and community partnerships to maintain public trust.

Public expectations of healthcare services continue to evolve. Communities increasingly expect healthcare to be accessible, responsive, digitally connected, and patient-centred. At the same time, national public health programmes continue to expand, requiring districts to implement new initiatives while maintaining existing essential services. Meeting these expectations without proportional increases in infrastructure, workforce, and financial resources may place additional pressure on healthcare systems.

Human resource sustainability remains another critical external challenge. Competition from the private healthcare sector and the surrounding oil and gas industry continues to affect recruitment and retention of healthcare professionals. Simultaneously, the retirement of experienced personnel may lead to the gradual loss of institutional knowledge, technical expertise, and leadership capacity if succession planning and workforce development are insufficient. These workforce pressures may reduce organisational resilience as public health demands continue to increase.

Digital transformation presents both opportunities and emerging risks. Greater dependence on electronic health systems, digital reporting platforms, and interconnected information systems improves efficiency but also increases vulnerability to cyber threats, data security issues, system failures, and technological obsolescence. Ensuring reliable digital infrastructure and cybersecurity will become increasingly important for maintaining continuity of public health operations.

Finally, the increasing complexity of public health challenges requires stronger collaboration beyond the health sector alone. Many future health determinants—including climate change, environmental sustainability, occupational safety, substance abuse, road safety, housing, education, urban planning, and industrial development—cannot be addressed solely by the healthcare system. Strengthening multisectoral governance, community participation, and partnerships with government agencies, academia, industry, and civil society will therefore be essential for protecting and improving population health.

Overall, the future public health landscape in Kemaman is expected to become increasingly dynamic and interconnected. Successfully addressing these external threats will require PKD Kemaman to strengthen surveillance systems, enhance emergency preparedness, invest in workforce development, embrace digital innovation, promote community resilience, and expand strategic partnerships so that the district remains capable of protecting the health of both its resident population and its highly mobile industrial community.
Additional Comments (Optional):
PKD transformation should not be viewed merely as organisational restructuring or the introduction of new programmes. Rather, it should represent a strategic shift towards building a more resilient, agile, data-driven, and people-centred public health system that is capable of responding to increasingly complex health challenges.

District Health Offices are the frontline of Malaysia's public health system. As the first level responsible for disease prevention, health protection, health promotion, emergency preparedness, and primary healthcare coordination, PKDs require sufficient authority, resources, and flexibility to respond effectively to local needs. While national policies provide overall direction, districts should be empowered to develop context-specific solutions based on their local epidemiology, demographic profile, available resources, and operational realities.

For districts such as Kemaman, future transformation should recognise that workload is influenced not only by resident population size but also by industrial activities, highly mobile populations, strategic economic assets, disaster risks, and geographical diversity. Resource allocation, workforce planning, infrastructure development, and performance indicators should therefore reflect service complexity rather than population figures alone.

Greater investment is also needed in modernising healthcare infrastructure, replacing ageing assets, strengthening digital health capabilities, and developing a sustainable workforce. At the same time, succession planning should become an integral component of PKD transformation to preserve institutional knowledge and ensure continuity of leadership as experienced personnel retire.

Future public health challenges—including climate change, emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance, behavioural health issues, substance misuse, population ageing, and rapid technological change—require multidisciplinary solutions that extend beyond the health sector. Strengthening collaboration with government agencies, local authorities, universities, industry partners, community organisations, and civil society should therefore remain a central pillar of PKD transformation.

Finally, it is hoped that future transformation initiatives will continue to strengthen the role of District Health Offices as the principal leaders of population health at district level. By empowering districts with appropriate resources, competent workforce, modern infrastructure, integrated digital systems, and greater operational flexibility, PKDs will be better positioned to deliver equitable, responsive, and sustainable public health services while protecting the health and well-being of all communities they serve.

QUESTION 5: THREATS AND EMERGING CHALLEN:
1. Emerging and Re-emerging Infectious Diseases
The emergence of new infectious diseases and the re-emergence of existing diseases remain significant threats. Increased human mobility and global travel can facilitate the rapid spread of diseases such as COVID-19, dengue, influenza, measles, and hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD).
Example:
•	A sudden increase in dengue cases following prolonged rainfall may require rapid epidemiological investigations, vector control activities, and public health education, placing considerable pressure on available manpower and resources. 
•	Imported infectious disease cases may require immediate surveillance, contact tracing, and risk communication to prevent community transmission.

2. Climate Change and Environmental Hazards
Climate change is expected to increase the frequency of extreme weather events, including floods, heatwaves, and prolonged rainy seasons. These conditions can influence disease transmission and disrupt public health services.
Example:
•	Flooding may contaminate water supplies, increase the risk of leptospirosis and waterborne diseases, and disrupt healthcare access in affected communities. 
•	Warmer temperatures and increased rainfall can expand mosquito breeding habitats, contributing to higher dengue incidence. 

3. Demographic Changes and Population Ageing
Malaysia's ageing population will increase demand for chronic disease management, preventive care, and community health services.
Example:
•	A growing elderly population may require expanded screening programmes, home-based care, vaccination services, and health promotion targeting healthy ageing, increasing workload for PKD and primary healthcare facilities. 

4. Rising Burden of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs)
The increasing prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and cancer presents a long-term public health challenge.
Example:
•	Greater demand for community-based screening, lifestyle intervention programmes, and long-term disease prevention initiatives may compete with communicable disease control activities for limited resources. 

5. Health Misinformation and Vaccine Hesitancy
The rapid spread of misinformation through social media can undermine public confidence in public health programmes.
Example:
•	False information regarding vaccine safety may reduce childhood immunisation uptake, increasing the risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles. 
•	During disease outbreaks, misinformation may discourage compliance with public health advice or encourage ineffective preventive measures. 

6. Resource and Workforce Constraints
Increasing programme complexity and public expectations may outpace available financial, human, and logistical resources.
Example:
•	Limited staffing may delay routine inspections, health promotion activities, and outbreak investigations when multiple public health incidents occur simultaneously. 
•	Budget limitations may restrict procurement of equipment, digital technologies, or additional field personnel. 

7. Migration and Population Mobility
Population movement, including migrant workers and transient populations, can complicate disease surveillance and continuity of care.
Example:
•	Mobile populations may be more difficult to reach for immunisation, tuberculosis screening, communicable disease follow-up, and health education, increasing the risk of delayed detection and ongoing transmission. 

8. Increasing Community Expectations
Communities increasingly expect rapid responses, transparent communication, and high-quality public health services.
Example:
•	Delays in responding to complaints about food safety, environmental sanitation, or vector control may reduce public trust and increase scrutiny through traditional and social media. 

9. Public Health Emergencies and Disasters
Natural disasters, industrial incidents, and other emergencies can disrupt routine health services and require rapid mobilisation of public health resources.
Example:
•	During severe flooding, PKD may need to establish temporary relief health services, conduct disease surveillance in evacuation centres, monitor water quality, and provide health education while maintaining essential routine public health programmes.

QUESTION 1: CURRENT FUNCTIONS AND DISTRI:
Pejabat Kesihatan Daerah (PKD) Pekan bertanggungjawab menyediakan perkhidmatan kesihatan awam merangkumi survelans penyakit, penjagaan kesihatan primer, keselamatan dan kualiti makanan, kesihatan persekitaran, serta kesihatan pekerjaan di seluruh 11 buah mukim dalam Daerah Pekan.

Keunikan profil kesihatan Daerah Pekan berbanding daerah lain di Pahang terletak pada beban penyakit (disease burden) yang tersendiri. Pekan mengendalikan kes penyakit tropika terabai (neglected tropical diseases) yang memerlukan perhatian khusus, seperti Kusta (Leprosy) dan Filariasis. Hal ini berkait rapat dengan demografi Pekan yang menempatkan populasi berisiko tinggi, iaitu komuniti Orang Asli terbesar di Negeri Pahang. Oleh kerana penyakit-penyakit ini kurang mendapat keutamaan di peringkat nasional, PKD Pekan berdepan cabaran kekangan sumber kewangan dan tenaga manusia.

Pada masa yang sama, PKD Pekan turut memikul beban ganda penyakit (dual burden of disease) berikutan peningkatan insiden penyakit tidak berjangkit (NCD) seperti diabetes, hipertensi, dan obesiti dalam kalangan penduduk setempat.
QUESTION 2: STRENGTHS:
Kekuatan utama Pejabat Kesihatan Daerah (PKD) Pekan berteraskan kepimpinan berwawasan dan berorientasikan penyelesaian masalah (solution-oriented leadership) dalam mendepani isu kesihatan awam utama di daerah ini.

PKD Pekan disokong oleh tenaga kerja yang kompeten dalam pencegahan, kawalan, dan pengurusan penyakit Kusta di peringkat Penjagaan Kesihatan Primer (primary care), di mana saringan kes disyaki (suspected cases) dilaksanakan secara komprehensif di semua Klinik Kesihatan. Selain itu, kebolehupayaan (versatility) warga kerja lapangan membolehkan pelaksanaan aktiviti bersasar seperti Night Blood Survey (NBS) dan pemetaan populasi berisiko dilaksanakan secara berkesan bagi pengesanan Filariasis.

Bagi memperkasakan kecekapan diagnostik dan klinikal, PKD Pekan melaksanakan program peningkatan kapasiti berasaskan bukti:

Pengukuhan Diagnostik Makmal: Penghantaran Juruteknologi Makmal Perubatan (JTMP) untuk latihan sangkut (attachment) di Makmal Kesihatan Awam Kebangsaan (MKAK) bagi meningkatkan kepakaran pengesanan Kusta.

Pemantapan Kemahiran Klinikal: Peningkatan kompetensi wajib bagi semua Penolong Pegawai Perubatan (PPP) dalam prosedur Pengambilan Calitan Kulit (Slit Skin Smear - SSS).

Melalui perancangan strategik di peringkat daerah serta kolaborasi merentas sektor bersama JAKOA, Pejabat Daerah dan Tanah, serta institusi pengajian tinggi, PKD Pekan berjaya mengoptimumkan penggunaan sumber yang terhad seterusnya meningkatkan kadar pengesanan kes Kusta dan Filariasis
QUESTION 3: WEAKNESSES:
Cabaran dan kelemahan utama yang dihadapi oleh Pejabat Kesihatan Daerah (PKD) Pekan berpusat pada kekangan sumber kewangan, logistik, dan rantaian bekalan ubat-ubatan.

Bagi kawalan penyakit Kusta, PKD Pekan telah mengenal pasti 18 Saku Endemik (Pockets of Endemicity - PoE) yang memerlukan program survelans berterusan selama lima (5) tahun. Pelaksanaan program Pengesanan Kes Aktif (Active Case Detection - ACD) di setiap PoE melibatkan kos operasional yang amat tinggi, terutamanya bagi tuntutan kerja lebih masa (OT), elaun perjalanan (mileage), serta pengurusan logistik program. Cabaran ini disukarkan lagi oleh faktor infrastruktur, merangkumi usia kenderaan pacuan empat roda (4WD) yang uzur, peralatan lapangan yang tidak diganti, serta modaliti diagnostik usang seperti mikroskop yang memerlukan penambahbaikan atau penggantian segera bagi mengekalkan kualiti saringan.

Manakala bagi penyakit Filariasis, PKD Pekan berdepan isu ketersediaan ubat-ubatan khusus. Buat masa ini, kawalan terpaksa dihadkan kepada aktiviti ACD dan rawatan kes yang disahkan sahaja.
